key_insight: A multimodal, task-specific digital motor assessment can distinguish Parkinson’s disease from healthy controls using a reduced set of MDS-UPDRS III upper-limb tasks and stable biomarkers.
clinical_relevance: This approach could support shorter, more objective, clinically anchored motor assessments if independently validated in broader patient populations.
method: 31 people with Parkinson’s disease and 30 age- and sex-matched healthy controls completed seven standardized MDS-UPDRS III tasks.
Researchers combined surface EMG, full-body inertial motion capture, and subject-specific musculoskeletal simulations.
A leakage-free machine-learning pipeline with cross-validation, permutation testing, task fusion, and stability-based biomarker selection was used.
evidence_signal: Pronunciation-supination showed the strongest single-task performance (ROC-AUC 0.94), and fused multimodal assessment remained high-performing (ROC-AUC 0.93; balanced accuracy 0.92).
watch_item: The findings come from a small cohort and require independent clinical validation before use in routine assessment.
paper_title: A Reduced Digital Motor Assessment using Multimodal Biomarkers in Parkinson's Disease
